title: Women's prayers
hookLine: Yiddish prayers by and for women, for candle-lighting, baking and childbirth

lines: A SOFT LITTLE BOOK ON THE SHELF.
cards: A small paperback, soft from use, with flour in the binding. It sits on a kitchen shelf in an old Polish town, next to the candlesticks. It wasn't in Hebrew.

It was in Yiddish, the language the woman of the house spoke to her children, her neighbors, the fishmonger. Inside: a prayer for lighting the Friday candles. A prayer for when the bread dough is ready.
A prayer for a woman in labor. A prayer for a sick child. Books like this one were kept close at hand, and read in the middle of the work.

teach.b: They're called tkhines. The word is the Hebrew techinah, a plea, a request for grace. It's the same word the psalmist uses for supplication: "The LORD hath heard my supplication; the LORD receiveth my prayer."

Tkhines were printed in Yiddish, in small books for the home. They were personal prayers, not part of the fixed service, and they were mostly for women, who often hadn't been taught Hebrew the way boys were.
Some were written by men. Some were written by women, and a few of their names survive.
Leah Horowitz wrote one asking the matriarchs, Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel and Leah, to plead for the people.

Other tkhines carry the name of a woman remembered as Sarah bas Tovim, though historians still debate how much of what carries her name is really hers. What strikes people now is where these prayers happen.

teach.h: AT THE STOVE, THE MIKVEH, THE GRAVE.
teach.b: At the stove. At the mikveh. At the cemetery.
At the moment a woman separates a piece of dough, the old commandment of challah, and the tkhine asks that the bread be blessed. The holy moments of the week weren't only in the sanctuary.
They were in the kitchen, timed to the rising of bread and the lighting of candles. Today scholars study them, and some people write new ones, in English and Hebrew, in the same spirit.

how: Tkhines were read privately, at home or in the women's section of the synagogue, at candle-lighting, separating challah, the mikveh, childbirth and cemetery visits; today they are studied by historians and some people write new personal prayers in their spirit.

games.q: it's Friday afternoon in a Yiddish-speaking town, long ago. the dough has risen and you're about to separate a piece of it. what's on the shelf beside you?
o: a little Yiddish book with a prayer for this exact moment.
nothing: prayer waits for the synagogue.
games.why: tkhine books had prayers for the dough, the candles, childbirth and more: the kitchen had its own holy moments.

practice: Pick something your hands can do for two minutes, wiping a counter, folding a towel, rinsing a cup, and do it slowly.

If you pray, say a line you know while you work, or ask in plain words that what you're tending be blessed; if not, let the chore have your whole attention, as if it mattered, the way it did to the women who kept these books.

wordCard.voice: Tkhine. A plea. A personal prayer in Yiddish, written mostly by and for women, for the holy moments of an ordinary week.
